newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Business bullish on HK, democracy not key - poll.
newsitem.headline: Business bullish on HK, democracy not key - poll.

text.p: Business professionals' confidence in the future of Hong Kong has risen substantially over the last year, reversing the downward trend of recent years, a poll released on Monday showed.
The survey also showed that maintaining a democratic system in Hong Kong was ranked as the least important factor for the the territory's business future.
Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30.

A poll taken by the Far Eastern Economic Review at its conference on the territory's future found that 92 percent of respondents said their personal view towards Hong Kong's future was "very positive" or "positive".
This compares with the downward trend of recent years.

Similar polls taken by the magazine over the last three years found that while 93 percent of business professionals were positive in 1994, only 84 percent were positive in 1995 and 76 percent in 1996.
Forty-nine percent of those surveyed this time said they were "very positive" about Hong Kong's future, compared with 41 percent in 1996.

The business executives said they were most worried about the legal system (51 percent), a slowdown in the economy (25 percent), a lower degree of autonomy (16 percent), lack of freedom of speech (13 percent) and higher taxes/duties (eight percent) after the handover.

The delegates also said the main factors making Hong Kong an attractive place to do business are its legal/business structure (38 percent), its role as the gateway to China (30 percent), its location (16 percent), its entrepreneurial spirit (13 percent) and its economic growth (12 percent).
The democratic system was the least important factor for business, with 35 percent of those polled agreeing.

The poll found that 92 percent of the delegates believed that freedom of information and press was crucial to Hong Kong's continued success, yet 75 percent of those polled thought this freedom would be reduced after the handover.
Almost all (92 percent) of those surveyed said their company's internal view does not differ from public attitudes this year, compared with 79 percent in 1996.
The magazine did not say how many people were polled or what the margin of error was.
